comments.text:
Below is some information by and about Huxley College professor David Clarke that first introduced me to the book above... he was an amazing man that changed my life in the best of ways. Beyond that,  I'm happy to see you got the older version with the original drawings.

From his memorial service up at  WWU

I am sitting on Church Mountain, at about 6200 feet.  The day is warm and unusually clear, and snow-capped Mt. Baker is a magnificent sight indeed.

Today I sat on a convenient rock and composed myself to meditate.  After two and a half hours of steady exertion with high heart rate and deep breathing, the body awareness was instantly one of ecstatic bliss... A sense of utter fulfillment in being alive, combined with a deep gratitude.  I sat dead still with closed eyes for perhaps half an hour, just rejoicing in all this, before directing my attention to wider issues--for it is here on Church Mountain that I have received inspiration and insight for many of my lectures.

Then a distress which has gripped me for some time suddenly melted away.  We treasure and love our affluence, yet if we are to avoid making our Earth uninhabitable we need to switch to a lifestyle of deliberate and extreme frugality.  My distress lay in my inability to see any way in which we could accomplish this transformation, and it melted away because now I had at least a part of the answer.  For I had complete happiness at little extra cost than the effort of a few hours of climbing, and the free time in which to do it!

I no longer doubt that there is life after death, and I believe that the way we live our lives and how we die has formative power over this afterlife.  I am convinced that there is much variety of life and consciousness in the Universe over and beyond the sum of our human lives, and that we are related to it and of consequence to it.  While we are alive, we have a creative role to play.  We are, so to speak, responsible to God and for God.  To die is in some way to enter this larger world of life and to embark on a further journey.  I see it as an enticing challenge.

Loved and admired by family, friends, and students, Dr. David E. Clarke of Bellingham died October 28 at his Bellingham home.  He died peacefully, surrounded by loved ones.  Born Feb. 16, 1920 to William and Margurite Clarke in Leicester, England, he has been a Bellingham resident since 1966.  He married Patricia Gray on Jan. 27 1968 in Seattle.  Dr. Clarke carried out military service in England with the Royal Engineers in 1941-1942.  Then elected to the Institution of Civil Engineers, he was employed by the Ministry of Town and Country Planning, Cambridge, England.  In 1952 he received a degree in Moral Sciences (Philosophy and Psychology) from Cambridge University, Cambridge, England.  Dr. Clarke then co-founded and taught at the Albert Schweitzer College in Switzerland.  Dr. Clarke came to the U.S. in 1958, received his Ph.D. in Political Science form Stanford University in 1964.  He came to Western Washington University in 1966 where he was appointed Associate Professor of Political Science.  In 1968 he was appointed half-time Associate Professor of Environmental Studies at Huxley College.  He has subsequently devoted his efforts to teaching about the environment and what we must do to prevent its collapse.  Dr. Clarke was an avid photographer, singer and mountaineer.  He had a keen wit, a love of beauty and a strong desire to teach others the importance of caring for our planet.  He will be deeply missed.  Survivors include his wife Pat; his daughter, Anna and his son Peter.   He is also survived by his brother Roger, who lives in Wales.  A memorial ceremony to celebrate his life will be held at 2:00 p.m. Saturday Nov. 5 in the concert hall of the Performing Arts Center at Western Washington University.  The service will be led by long-time friend John Quirk.  Memorials may be made to the David Clarke Graduate Fellowship, Political Science Department, Western Washington University, Bellingham, Washington 98225.
 
(Plaque on bench, Boulevard Park)
David E Clarke
1920-1994
Mountain Man & Philosopher
He dedicated his life
to teaching a new
paradigm for global survival.
Now it’s in our hands.
